name: Malignancy (B-symptoms)

matching.reasoningTemplate: Weight loss, night sweats and lymphadenopathy raise concern for lymphoma or other malignancy.

redFlags: Persistent unexplained B-symptoms warrant urgent workup

clinicalPearls: B symptoms are formally defined for lymphoma staging (the Ann Arbor 'B' suffix) as unexplained fever (>38C), drenching night sweats, and/or unexplained weight loss exceeding 10% of body weight over the 6 months before diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.861, p.869).
The tempo of symptoms helps separate aggressive from indolent lymphoma: rapid symptomatic progression and the presence of B symptoms suggest a more aggressive process (Harrison 22e p.903).
Among malignancies, lymphoma is by far the commonest cause of malignancy-related fever of unknown origin, and the fever can precede any palpable lymphadenopathy (Harrison 22e p.193).

About one-third of patients with classical Hodgkin lymphoma present with B symptoms; Hodgkin disease can even present as a fever of unknown origin, more often in older patients with abdominal mixed-cellularity disease (Harrison 22e p.869).
Pel-Ebstein fever (cyclical fever lasting days to weeks alternating with afebrile intervals) is a rare but classic Hodgkin lymphoma presentation (Harrison 22e p.869).

Node character matters: lymphomatous nodes tend to be large, firm, rubbery, mobile, symmetric and non-tender, whereas metastatic carcinoma nodes are typically hard, non-tender and fixed to surrounding tissue (Harrison 22e p.477).

Supraclavicular and scalene node enlargement is always abnormal and warrants prompt evaluation; a left supraclavicular node (Virchow node) classically reflects a gastrointestinal primary, but lung, breast, testis and ovarian cancers also seed these nodes (Harrison 22e p.477).

Examination in suspected lymphoma should systematically cover all peripheral nodal sites plus Waldeyer ring, liver and spleen size, effusions/ascites, and testicular, breast or skin involvement, since any of these can change staging and management (Harrison 22e p.903).

Enlarged intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal nodes are usually malignant (lymphoma, or germ-cell tumour in young men), in contrast to the largely benign causes of cervical adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.477).

Half of all cancer patients lose some weight and up to 20% of cancer deaths are attributable directly to cachexia; malignancy that declares itself through marked weight loss generally carries a poor prognosis (Harrison 22e p.317).
harrison.pathophysiology: B symptoms in lymphoma are cytokine-mediated systemic effects of the tumour rather than direct mass effects. In classical Hodgkin lymphoma the malignant Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg cells are rare within a tumour mass that is largely a polyclonal inflammatory infiltrate reacting to tumour-derived cytokines; this inflammatory milieu drives constitutional symptoms and contributes to the generalised immune suppression seen in these patients. Involuntary weight loss in malignancy reflects a combination of anorexia, sarcopenia and a cytokine-driven cachexia syndrome. (Harrison 22e p.316, p.869)
additionalDifferentials: Hodgkin lymphoma (classical) - nontender cervical/supraclavicular/axillary nodes, frequent mediastinal involvement (Harrison 22e p.869)
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma - nodal and extranodal disease; B symptoms part of staging (Harrison 22e p.860)
Acute or chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (can produce generalised adenopathy and constitutional symptoms) (Harrison 22e p.476)
Richter transformation of CLL - rapidly progressive focal adenopathy with night sweats, fever, weight loss and high LDH (Harrison 22e p.897)
Metastatic carcinoma to nodes (head/neck, lung, breast, thyroid, GI primaries) (Harrison 22e p.477)
Germ-cell tumour (retroperitoneal nodes in young men) (Harrison 22e p.477)
Occult solid tumours presenting with involuntary weight loss - GI/hepatobiliary, lung, breast, genitourinary, ovarian, prostate (Harrison 22e p.317)
infectionMimics: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV or CMV) - generalised adenopathy with constitutional symptoms (Harrison 22e p.476)
Tuberculosis - can cause unilateral mediastinal adenopathy and mesenteric lymphadenitis mimicking lymphoma, with night sweats and weight loss (Harrison 22e p.477)
Histoplasmosis - unilateral paratracheal node involvement that can mimic lymphoma in endemic regions (Harrison 22e p.477)
HIV / AIDS - generalised lymphadenopathy and a recognised lymphoma risk factor (Harrison 22e p.476, p.903)
nonInfectiousMimics: Sarcoidosis - mediastinal/hilar adenopathy and constitutional symptoms (Harrison 22e p.477)
Systemic lupus erythematosus and mixed connective tissue disease - generalised adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.476)
Drug-induced (phenytoin/diphenylhydantoin and others) lymphadenopathy, including DRESS/DIHS with eosinophilia and extensive adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.193, p.476)
Castleman disease, Kikuchi histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis, Rosai-Dorfman disease, angioimmunoblastic lymphadenopathy, IgG4-related disease (Harrison 22e p.476)
additionalInvestigations: Excisional biopsy of the largest abnormal node is preferred; fine-needle aspiration should NOT be the first procedure as it usually yields insufficient tissue and delays diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.478)
Serum protein electrophoresis to detect a monoclonal paraprotein (Harrison 22e p.903)
Serum beta2-microglobulin and LDH - independent prognostic markers in NHL (Harrison 22e p.903)
CBC with differential, comprehensive metabolic/liver panel, uric acid and calcium (Harrison 22e p.317, p.904)
ESR and CRP as part of the constitutional-symptom / weight-loss workup (Harrison 22e p.316, p.869)
Contrast CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis for staging; FDG-PET/CT preferred for aggressive lymphomas and Hodgkin lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.904)
Bone marrow biopsy where indicated; lumbar puncture if CNS-risk histology or neurologic features (Harrison 22e p.903-904)
HIV and hepatitis B and C serology - risk factors for NHL and relevant to hepatitis B reactivation risk (Harrison 22e p.904)
Cervical node ultrasound long-to-short axis ratio (<2.0 favours malignancy) where head/neck cancer is suspected (Harrison 22e p.478)
Age/sex/risk-appropriate cancer screening (e.g. faecal occult blood, colonoscopy, mammography) and abdominal ultrasound in occult-malignancy weight-loss workup (Harrison 22e p.318)
redFlags: Supraclavicular or scalene adenopathy - always abnormal, biopsy promptly (Harrison 22e p.477-478)
Solitary hard non-tender cervical node in an older tobacco user - prompt biopsy after ENT mucosal assessment (Harrison 22e p.478)
Node size >2 cm with an abnormal chest x-ray in younger patients - predicts malignant/granulomatous biopsy yield (Harrison 22e p.521)
Hard fixed nodes, or firm mobile generalised adenopathy suggestive of lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.478)
Airway, oesophageal or SVC compression from thoracic adenopathy (cough/wheeze, hoarseness, dysphagia, facial/arm/neck swelling) (Harrison 22e p.520)
Enlarged intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal nodes (usually malignant) (Harrison 22e p.477)
Involuntary weight loss >=5% over 6 months prompting structured malignancy workup (Harrison 22e p.358)
harrison.prognosis: Lymphoma prognosis is stage- and biology-dependent. For NHL the International Prognostic Index uses five factors (age >=60, elevated LDH, ECOG performance status >=2, Ann Arbor stage III/IV, and >1 extranodal site); for DLBCL treated with R-CHOP, 0 factors gives ~94% 4-year survival versus ~53% with 3-5 factors. Across lymphomas, decreased outcome is associated with B symptoms, advanced stage, elevated LDH and bulky disease (e.g. lymph-node mass >7 cm). In occult solid malignancy, presentation through significant involuntary weight loss generally carries a very poor prognosis, whereas when no cause is found after thorough workup the prognosis is comparatively favourable. (Harrison 22e p.317, p.861, NHL prognosis section)
pitfalls: Do NOT give glucocorticoids for undiagnosed lymphadenopathy - their lympholytic effect can obscure lymphoma, leukaemia and Castleman disease and delay/disrupt diagnosis (the rare exception is life-threatening pharyngeal obstruction from Waldeyer-ring tissue in mononucleosis) (Harrison 22e p.521).

Fine-needle aspiration is inadequate for an initial lymphoma diagnosis - obtain an excisional/core biopsy; FNA is reserved for thyroid nodules and confirming relapse of a known cancer (Harrison 22e p.478).
Antibiotics are NOT indicated for lymphadenopathy unless there is strong evidence of bacterial infection (Harrison 22e p.521).
Localized-versus-generalized adenopathy has limited discriminatory value because many causes produce either pattern; do not over-rely on it (Harrison 22e p.476).

In primary care most lymphadenopathy is benign (>two-thirds nonspecific/URI, <1% malignant) and needs only short-interval follow-up - but persistent or enlarging nodes must be re-evaluated and biopsied (Harrison 22e p.476, p.521).
If a head-and-neck primary is suspected behind a solitary cervical node, perform a careful ENT exam and biopsy any suspicious mucosal lesion first before excising the node (Harrison 22e p.478).
harrison.severityClassification: Ann Arbor staging (stages I-IV) with suffix A (no systemic symptoms) or B (presence of B symptoms: fever >38C, drenching night sweats, or weight loss >10% body weight over preceding 6 months); suffix E for localized extralymphatic extension. B-symptom status (the A/B designation) and stage drive prognosis and therapy. (Harrison 22e p.861, p.869)
